title: CLINICAL FEATURES AND EFFECT OF PRIMARY BILE ACIDS IN CHILDREN WITH 3‐BETA‐HYDROXY‐D5‐C27‐STEROID DEHYDROGENASE/ISOMERASE DEFICIENCY DIAGNOSED AT DIFFERENT AGES
abstract: 3β-hydroxy-D5-C27-steroid dehydrogenase/isomerase (3β-HSD) deficiency causes severe cholestasis and chronic liver disease. Prompt identification and treatment avoid the progression of the disease. We aimed to define its natural history and response to treatment at different ages. Four patients diagnosed by tandem mass spectrometry and monitored by liver function tests (LFTs) and urinary 3β,7α dihydroxy-5-cholenoic acid (3β,7α DH5C) that was increased in all at diagnosis. GGT was normal in all. Patient 1 was initially started on ursodehoxycholic acid (UDCA) for 2.5 years. All 4, upon diagnosis, received 10 mg/kg/day of a combination of UDCA and chenodehoxycholic acid (CDCA). Patient 1 presented at 2.5 months of age with giant cell hepatitis, was initially misdiagnosed and started on UDCA with prompt normalisation of liver function tests (LFTs). At 2.5 years of age, the time of diagnosis, a second liver biopsy showed worsened fibrosis. Following the start of CDCA urinary 3β,7α DH5C normalised, and a further follow up biopsy showed no progression of fibrosis. Patient 2 (sibling of pt 1) was diagnosed at birth. LFTs were normal. The child, started on UDCA and CDCA, normalised 3β,7α DH5C levels and has minimal inflammation at liver biopsy at the age of 4 years. Patient 3 had a history of jaundice, hepatomegaly, bleeding during her stay in Morocco. She presented at 7 years of age with INR 1.4, normal bilirubin, and ALT, low GGT, and had biopsy proven cirrhosis. Following treatment 3β,7α DH5C normalised. Patient 4 (sibling of pt 3) presented with failure to thrive, jaundice with acholic stools, hepato-splenomegaly, severe coagulopathy (INR 2.3), ALT 329 U/l, GGT 30 and biopsy proven cirrhosis. After treatment he cleared jaundice, INR is 1.4, ALT 57; 3β,7α DH5C disappeared. β-hydroxy-D5-C27-steroid dehydrogenase/isomerase should be suspected at any paediatric age in patients with chronic liver disease and low GGT, whatever the severity of cholestasis and coagulopathy. Treatment with CDCA corrects the defect improving and stabilising liver disease.

title: GROWTH AND INTESTINAL FUNCTION 3 TO 16 YEARS AFTER INTESTINAL TRANSPLANTATION
abstract: To study the absorptive function of the transplanted intestine on the long term. from 1994, among 65 transplanted children, 24 (5 girls) were followed more than 2 years with a functional graft. A girl transplanted in 1989 is also included. The graft is an isolated intestine (7), plus the liver (18), plus the colon (12). Median follow-up is 6 years (2-16). Treatment is tacrolimus and prednisone (<0.2 mg/kg) on alternate days. Serum markers of malnutrition, stool components and biopsies were controlled. all patients were weaned from parenteral nutrition. PN was re-instituted in 2, 8 y post-transplantation for chronic rejection (non compliance), and 6 y post-transplantation for a fistula secondary to surgery for occlusion. The mean caloric intake is 20% more than recommended for age. Enteral nutrition is needed in 13/25 at 2 y, 5/18 at 5 y (2 severe anorexia). Three still have an ileostomy. Growth velocity is normal, 8/25 have a growth curve <− 2 SD for height, 3/4 adults have a normal final height. Weight is normal for height. The global and fat absorption rates are 88/80 % at 2y, 86/76 % at 5 y, 84/68 % at 7 y (only 3 patients). Pancreatic function is normal. Pancreatic enzyme supplementation does not modify the growth velocity. Cholesterol is low (3.1 mM), vitamins ADE are normal with supplements, coagulation is normal. In biopsies, intestinal villi are normal. Inflammation is moderate to important in 3/9 2 y, 3/5 7 y, 2/3 10 y, 0/1 15 y post-transplantation., predominating in the colon. the absorptive function is adequate to support growth. Steatorrhea may be due to persistent lymphangiectasia. Final height will probably be normal, with a high caloric intake and delayed puberty. Late graft loss is rare. Inflammation should be followed (chronic rejection ? risk of cancer ?). the functional results of intestinal transplantation are satisfactory on the mid-and long-term.

title: THE AETIOLOGY AND MANAGEMENT OF EXTRA HEPATIC PORTAL VEIN OBSTRUCTION IN CHILDREN: A SINGLE CENTRE EXPERIENCE
abstract: To study predisposing factors, presenting features, management and long-term outcome of extra hepatic portal vein obstruction (EHPVO). The medical records of 108 children (67 male, median age 4.75 [range 1 day-16.3] years) with EHPVO between Jan 1979 and Sept 2005 were reviewed retrospectively. Median follow up period was 6 [range 0.39-19.5] years. Clinical, haematological and biochemical features on presentation, management of bleeding and long term outcome were recorded. Predisposing factors like umbilical line catheterization, peritoneal sepsis were identified in 14 (13%) and 9 (8%). Detailed investigations into procoagulant states were available in 30 patients: protein C was low in 6, protein S was slightly low in 2 and factor V Leiden heterozygosity was seen in 1. Clinical presentation included splenomegaly in 91%, ascites in 4%. Abnormal liver enzymes and INR were seen in 13 and 14 children respectively. Haematological parameters of hypersplenism were present in 13 (12%). Bleeding occurred in 83 (77%) patients, for whom it was the presenting feature in 78 (94%). Median age at first bleeding was 4.58 years [range 0.02-16.37]. On first endoscopy oesophageal varices were present in 92 (93%) patients, 70 (76%) received sclerotherapy, 5 (5%) were banded and 16 (17%) both. Six [1-20] sclerotherapy or 2 [1-5] banding sessions were required to eradicate the varices. Complications of endoscopy occurred in 34 (37%) patients: esophageal ulcers in 16, esophageal stricture in 10, ulcers and strictures in 7 and erosive gastritis in 1. 17 (16%) children underwent shunt surgery for uncontrolled bleeding at a median age of 9.7 [range, 5.2-23.7] and the shunt is functioning in 8 patients at a follow up of 12.8 [2.3-19.5] years. All those with non-functioning shunts had gastrointestinal bleeding which was controlled with sclerotherapy in 7. One required liver transplantation and one had a second shunt operation which was successful. The aetiology of EHPVO in most children remains unknown. Sclerotherapy and banding are an effective treatment for bleeding varices with good long term outcome.

title: THE NATURAL HISTORY OF COW'S MILK PROTEIN SENSITISATION IN INFANTILE ALLERGIC COLITIS CONSTIPATION‐ AN ASSOCIATION WITH MULTIPLE FOOD ALLERGY?
abstract: To document the clinical outcome and evidence of persisting dietary sensitisation, in particular, cow's milk protein (CMP), in infants with allergic colitis (AC). We carried out a prospective study with comprehensive evaluation of immunological (1), endoscopic, clinical profiles and follow up for assessment of in vivo/in vitro evidence of CMP sensitivity. 12 AC infants were diagnosed, median onset at 6 weeks (2 days-7 months). Clinical cow's milk sensitivity was defined by resolution of bloody diarrhoea on CMP exclusion (with maternal dairy exclusion or amino acid formula) and subsequent rechallenge (open in breast fed, double blind challenge in amino acid formula fed). Clinical reactions to sequential dietary antigen introduction during weaning (soya/wheat/egg etc.) were documented. 10/12 had CMP sensitivity, 5/10 showed positive Th1/Th2 blood mononuclear responses (IFN-γ, IL-4, IL-5 cytokine production by ELISPOT to casein and/or beta-lactoglobulin), 3 with Th2 lamina propria CMP responses. 9/10 CMP sensitive AC infants were followed up to median 23 months (8-34 months). One infant was lost to follow-up before CMP rechallenge. CMP was tolerated in 3 cases by 12 months, 1 case by 18 months and 2 cases by 24 months. 3 cases were still CMP sensitive at 21, 23 and 34 months. Multiple food allergy (≥2 antigens) with positive gastrointestinal reactions and/or cutaneous manifestations, both immediate and delayed onset, were observed in 6 CMP sensitive cases (soya, n = 5; eggs, n = 3; others, n = 2; none to wheat). Unrestricted diet was achieved in just 4/8 CMP sensitive AC infants in the follow-up period. In this group of AC with early CMP sensitisation, the clinical resolution and dietary tolerance were variable and often delayed. Although this may reflect a selective populaton, it highlights the importance of longer term dietary follow-up despite CMP tolerance by age one year.

title: FOCAL VILLOUS ATROPHY OF THE DUODENUM IN CHILDREN WHO HAVE OUTGROWN COW'S MILK ALLERGY H BIOACTIVE MILK FAT GLOBULE MEMBRANE PROTEINS ‐ CHROMOENDOSCOPY AND MAGNIFICATION ENDOSCOPY EVALUATION
abstract: Patchy villous atrophy of duodenal mucosa has been described in young children with cows's milk allergy (CMA). Cows's milk protein-sensitive enteropathy may persist in older children and shows characteristic histological features. The advent of magnification endoscopy may allow the macroscopic detection of unrecognized villous atrophy in these patients. The aim of the study was to evaluate the duodenum mucosa in older children with cow's milk allergy in infancy using chromoendoscopy and magnification endoscopy. The study involved 15 children (9 girls; mean aged 15 years; range 12-18) with CMA diagnosed and treated in infancy, currently on normal diet, referred to our department due to abdominal pain. The control group consisted of 8 children with abdominal pain without any evidence of allergy (5 girls, mean age 15 years, range 13-18). In all patients the chromoendoscopy was performed with a magnification endoscope (GIFQ 160Z, Olympus) and videotaped for detailed analysis. For staining 1% solution of methylene blue was sprayed over the mucosa. All examination were conducted under general anesthesia. The bulb and the descending portion of the duodenum was examined. Pathological findings were defined as focal villous atrophy. Seven of 15 patients (47%) with CMA in infancy had focal villous atrophy of the descending part of the duodenum. In 1 patient erosions of bulb were present. In the control group, the villous atrophy was seen in 1 case (12.5%). This is the first study demonstrating by magnification endoscopy that in children who have outgrown cow's milk allergy the patchy villous atrophy of the duodenum is a common finding. Magnification endoscopy may be useful for detecting mucosal abnormalitis, delineating there extent, and allowing target.

title: EFFECTS OF REDUCING THE PROTEIN QUANTITY AND RENAL SOLUTE LOAD OF INFANT FORMULA ON FORMULA INTAKE, GROWTH, PLASMA AMINO ACIDS AND INSULIN
abstract: To compare intake, growth and blood chemistry between a group of breast-fed infants and three groups of infants fed formulas differing in the amount and quality of protein and in potential renal solute load (PRSL). Breast-fed and formula-fed infants differ in energy and protein intake, growth rate, plasma amino acids and blood urea nitrogen (BUN). We hypothesized that these differences may be due to protein quantity/quality or PRSL (thirst). Double-blind randomized controlled trial of formula-fed (FF) infants (n=84) fed a) control formula (14 g pro/L; 20:80) (C), b) modified protein quality formula (14 g pro/L; 60:40) (MP) or c) low protein (12 g pro/L 0-2 mo, 11 g pro/L 2-5 mo; 60:40), low PRSL formula (LP). A comparison group of exclusively breast-fed (BF) infants (n=73) was included. Infants from Fairfield and Vacaville, CA were recruited at 2-4 wks of age and followed until 5 mo. Growth was monitored monthly, intake was measured at 1, 3 and 5 mo, and blood samples were drawn at 5 mo. Plasma amino acids, BUN and insulin were assayed. There were no sign differences among the FF groups in growth, formula intake or plasma insulin, so for this analysis the 3 groups were combined for comparisons with the BF group. The BF group was significantly lower than the FF groups in weight and length gain 1-5 mo, milk intake at 1, 3 and 5 mo, plasma insulin at 5 mo (42.6 ± 25.8 vs 65.4 ± 31.7 pmol/L, p=0.001) and plasma insulin-releasing amino acids at 5 mo (967 ± 178 vs 1133 ± 298 umol/L, p<0.01). Altering the amount and/or quality of protein in formula (and PRSL) to be more similar to breast milk did not significantly affect intake or growth. Intake and growth were significantly lower in BF than in FF infants, regardless of type of formula used. BF infants had lower plasma insulin and insulin-releasing amino acids than FF infants. The higher energy intake and growth of FF infants relative to BF infants is due to factors other than the protein and PRSL content of infant formula.

title: GOS & FOS PLAY A PROTECTIVE ROLE VS NEONATAL JAUNDICE
abstract: To examine whether supplementing formula with oligosaccharide mixture may modulate bilirubin total (BT) levels in formula fed infants during the first weeks of life by modification of intestinal microflora. Fifty healthy full-term infants were double blind randomly allocated into two groups to receive either supplementation of oligosacharides mixture producted by Numico Research (GOS/FOS ratio 9:1) at the dosage of 0.8 g/100ml (n = 27) or placebo (maltodexrine) (n = 23), from birth through the first 28 days of life. BT (TcB) level was determined by multiwavelength spectral analysis, (BiliCheck device SpectRx Inc Norcross, GA) within 2 hours after birth (T0), at 24, 48, 72 h and at completed 5, 7, 10, 28 (T8) days of life. Capillary hematocrit (HT) was further determined by conventional methods. Groups were comparable for birth weight, gestational age, maternal age, type of delivery, baseline (T0) serum* TcB level (mean [SD; range], gos-fos 3.0 [0.7; 2.1-4.8] vs. placebo 3.0 [0.8; 1.6-5.0] mg/dl, and HT level. Pattern of TcB significantly differed between groups through the study (P < 0.01; Anova for repeated measures). Infants in supplemented group exhibited lower plasma TcB levels than placebo group from 72 h of life onwards (P < 0.02). At T8, mean [SD; range] TcB level was 2.4 [0.5; 1.1-3.6] mg/dl (gos-fos) vs. 2.8 [0.4; 1.8-3.8] mg/dl (placebo). HT significantly decreased from birth to day 28 in both groups (P < 0.0001) but no difference between groups was found (P > 0.55). In formula fed infants, supplementation of a mixture of gos-fos significantly lowers bilirubin level after 72 hours of life. It may be hypothesize that stimulating the intestinal growth of bifidobacteria and lactobacilli enhances bilirubin excretion by reducing it to urobilinoids. Larger randomized trials would be of interest to evaluate prophylactic and therapeutic use of gos-fos in neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia.

title: OCCURRENCE OF TYPE 1 DIABETES TOGETHER WITH CELIAC DISEASE IS NOT ASSOCIATED WITH MBL DEFICIENCY
abstract: Mannan-binding lectin (MBL) is a pattern recognition molecule involved in the innate immune system, able to differentiate between the carbohydrates found on self glycoproteins and the carbohydrate patterns found on infectious non-self surfaces. MBL deficiency seems to increase the susceptibility to chronic inflammation and certain autoimmune diseases and an increased frequency has been reported in celiac disease (CD).. We tested the hypothesis that MBL deficiency is associated with the development of Type 1 diabetes (T1D) in patients with CD. A population sample of a total of 79 patients (all HLA-DQ2 and/or HLA-DQ8) of Caucasian ethnicity (1-15 years of age) with CD of whom 41 had associated T1D and an age-matched control group of children with T1D (n=48) were investigated. Polymorphisms in exon 1 of the MBL-2 gene were detected by direct sequencing using ABI PRISM BigDye Terminator v3.1 Cycle Sequencing Kit (Applied Biosystems) and an ABI Prism 3100 Genetic Analyzer (Applied Biosystems). There were no differences in the frequency of structural mutation homozygotes or compound heterozygotes (O/O) between CD patients (n = 38) and CD patients with associated T1D (n = 41) (P = 0.91; Odds Ratio: 0.92 (95% CI: 0.21-3.97)). The frequency of O/O in all CD patients (CD and CD with associated T1D combined; n = 79) was approximately twice as high as the frequency in patients with T1D alone (n = 48) (0.10 and 0.04, respectively). This difference was not significant (P = 0.22; Odds Ratio: 2.59 (95% CI: 0.53-12.75)). Examination of the three mutant alleles of the MBL gene causing MBL deficiency in patients with CD and CD patients with associated T1D revealed that MBL deficiency is not a risk factor for the occurrence of T1D in CD patients.

title: COMPARISON OF THE EFFECT OF CORNSTARCH THICKENED FORMULA AND STRENGTHENED REGULAR FORMULA ON REGURGITATION, GASTRIC EMPTYING AND NUTRITIONAL STATUS IN INFANTILE REGURGITATION
abstract: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of cornstarch-supplemented formula on clinical symptoms, gastric emptying and nutritional status in infants with regurgitation. We performed a prospective randomised trial evaluating the therapeutic efficacy of two different formula feedings (cornstarch-thickened formula, group A; 25 % strengthened formula, group B) in 81 young infants with regurgitation/vomiting ≥ 3 times/day. A Tc-99m milk scintigraphy was performed at inclusion and after 2 months to quantify the number of reflux episodes and gastric emptying time; all studied infants underwent a 2-month period of clinical follow-up evaluating regurgitation and body weight gain. At inclusion, group A and B had a similar age and weight. After the two-month period of intervention, regurgitation and vomiting had both more decreased (both p < 0.001 at 1 and 2 month) in group A than in group B. Non-regurgitation symptoms (irritability, cough, choking, night awake) decreased (p = 0.045 at 1 month and 0.017 at 2 months) and weight increased (p<0.01 at 1 and 2 months) in group A as compared to group B. Gastric emptying improved significantly in group A as compared with group B (all p < 0.001 for T1/2, and residual volume at 60 and 90 minutes). Ingested feeding volume was significantly larger in the group receiving cornstarch-thickened formula. Cornstarch-thickened formula feeding decreases the frequency of regurgitation/vomiting, provides better body weight gain and has an accelerated gastric emptying in comparison to a 25 % strengthened regular formula in infants with regurgitation.
